metadata.title: Teachers’ perceived societal appreciation: PISA outcomes predict whether teachers feel valued in society

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, ISCED 2) with a multistage sampling design: schools selected with systematic random sampling and probability proportional to size (PPS) within explicit country strata, and teachers randomly selected within schools. The manuscript reports that TALIS requires minimum response rates (≥75% of selected schools; at least the principal and 50% of teachers participating) to ensure comparability, but it does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any specific weight variable names in the analysis. Because the dependent variable is a TALIS Likert-scale measure and the models are multilevel regressions (not ML algorithms), the paper’s weighting strategy is not transparently documented; therefore, it is unclear whether complex survey weights were applied to produce population-representative estimates. The analytic sample is defined by listwise deletion of cases with missing values on analysis variables, and continuous predictors are group-mean centered at the school level (and for the school-level disadvantaged background at the country mean), which affects interpretation of coefficients even if weights were not used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variable is teachers’ perceived societal appreciation (PSA) measured via TALIS Likert-scale items, not a cognitive achievement score for which PISA provides plausible values. The paper does use PISA outcomes as country-level predictors (scores/ranks derived from OECD publications), but the PSA outcome itself is not PV-based. Missing data handling is addressed via deletion of cases with missing values on variables included in the analyses, so PV-specific missing-data procedures are not relevant here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses TALIS 2018 wave data for lower secondary education (ISCED 2). Schools are selected using systematic random sampling with probability proportional to size (PPS) within explicit country strata (e.g., type of funding), and teachers are randomly selected within participating schools. The final multilevel analytic sample includes 25 countries/regions and 66,593 teachers across 4,307 schools. The authors delete cases with missing values for one or more variables included in the analyses (listwise deletion). Continuous individual-level variables are group-mean centered using the school mean; the school-level disadvantaged background percentage is group-mean centered using the country mean.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (2018) Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — Perceived societal appreciation (PSA)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear regression (standardized coefficients, Table 2). Satisfaction with salary: β=0.24 (p≤0.001). Job satisfaction: β=0.10 (p≤0.001). Teacher self-efficacy: β=0.02 (p≤0.001). Participation in school policy: β=0.07 (p≤0.001). PISA score (Science): β=0.14+ (p≤0.10).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Lower secondary, ISCED 2) the study leveraged satisfaction with salary, job satisfaction, teacher self-efficacy, participation in school policy, and PISA score (Science) to predict teachers’ perceived societal appreciation (PSA), finding that satisfaction with salary was the strongest individual-level predictor (β=0.24, p≤0.001) and that higher country PISA science performance was positively associated with PSA (β=0.14, p≤0.10). This indicates that improving teachers’ perceived material security and aligning public narratives with international performance trends may help sustain teachers’ sense of societal value, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (2018) Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — Change in PSA (2018 vs 2013)
main_findings.target_variable: Change in perceived societal appreciation (PSA) between 2013 and 2018
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlations (Table 3). Change in PSA vs PISA score change: Science r=0.14 (p=0.26, one-tailed), Maths r=0.06 (p=0.39), Reading r=0.23 (p=0.14). Trend in PISA score change: Science r=0.30 (p=0.08), Maths r=0.24 (p=0.12), Reading r=0.42 (p=0.02). Mean correlation across 20 PISA-change indicators: 0.29; 14/20 correlations significant (one-tailed; p<0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Lower secondary, ISCED 2) data to relate within-country changes, the study leveraged changes in PISA outcomes (Science, Maths, Reading) to predict changes in teachers’ perceived societal appreciation (PSA) from 2013 to 2018, finding that decreases in PISA outcomes were associated with decreases in PSA and that the average correlation across 20 PISA-change operationalizations was 0.29 with 14/20 significant (one-tailed; p<0.01). This indicates that public communication and policy attention tied to international test trends may influence teachers’ collective morale and retention-relevant perceptions, even if the exact direction and strength vary by how PISA change is operationalized.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, ISCED 2) teacher survey data from 25 countries/regions, 4,307 schools, and 66,593 teachers, with PSA measured on a 4-point Likert scale. It estimates three-level multilevel linear regression models (teacher, school, country) and reports standardized coefficients (Table 2), showing that satisfaction with salary is the strongest individual-level correlate of PSA (β=0.24, p≤0.001), while job satisfaction (β=0.10, p≤0.001) and participation in school policy (β=0.07, p≤0.001) also relate positively. At the country level, higher PISA science performance is positively associated with PSA (β=0.14, p≤0.10), with similar patterns for other PISA domains but weaker statistical support. For within-country change, correlations between PSA change (2018 vs 2013) and multiple PISA-change indicators yield a mean correlation of 0.29 and 14/20 significant correlations (one-tailed; p<0.01). The paper is correlational (no causal identification) and does not document survey-weight usage; additionally, PSA is not PV-based, so PV handling is not applicable.
